Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, military/police uniforms are not a plausible primary trigger unless there is additional trauma context; this item points to an interpersonal/authority-related trauma theme not represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names
issues.explanation: 'Hearing related names' is hard to reconcile with natural disaster as the index trauma unless a specific deceased/injured person is central, which is not supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal intruder/assailant threat rather than disaster-related danger, creating a cross-node mismatch with the trauma type and trigger/memory content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: Feeling safe only in a very limited number of places can occur in PTSD, but here it clusters with home-intruder monitoring and touch avoidance into an interpersonal-danger profile that is poorly matched to natural disaster trauma.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item implies fear of an intruder or interpersonal attack in the home, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma profile. With flooding/water triggers present, the expected threat would be environmental danger rather than someone entering the home.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no negative-appraisal items about personal blame, humiliation, or moral failure that would make shame a coherent central memory response.

issues.item: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding all physical contact is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma and is not clinically well linked to the reported disaster-related triggers and memory items. It addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in the profile.

vignette:
Marisol had lived in the same coastal town in Florida for twenty-two years when Hurricane Idalia made landfall. She had ridden out storms before - boarded windows, filled bathtubs, waited - but nothing had prepared her for the night the surge came. The water rose faster than any forecast had promised, and within forty minutes her ground floor was submerged to the ceiling. She remembers clinging to a door frame in the dark, the roar filling everything, the particular smell of salt and sewage mixed together, and the moment she watched her neighbor's car float past her second-floor window like a toy. She was rescued the following morning, hypothermic and mute, sitting on her roof. That was fourteen months ago. She is fifty-seven years old, divorced, and she has not been the same since.

In the weeks after the hurricane, Marisol returned to her work as a physical therapist at an outpatient rehabilitation clinic. She told herself that routine would help. It did not. The clinic is located two blocks from a retention pond, and on her walk from the parking lot she passes it every morning. The first time she saw the water's surface ripple in the wind, her stomach turned over with a nausea so sudden and complete that she had to grip a fence post. That visceral physical response - the same one she had felt the night the surge came - pulled the memory back with it: not as a coherent recollection, but as a flood of sensation without image, the full emotional weight of that night pressing into her chest while she stood in bright daylight beside a perfectly ordinary pond. She began parking on the opposite side of the building.

The memory itself is strange to her in ways she finds hard to articulate. She says it feels like something that happened to another woman - someone she knows about but cannot quite locate inside herself. Yet that dissociative quality offers no protection, because without warning she can be overtaken by the emotion of it entirely: a grief so overwhelming it stops her breath, arriving without any accompanying picture, as though the feeling has detached from its own story and learned to travel alone. When the memory does surface - triggered by the sight of water, or by the nausea that precedes it, or by hearing someone mention a name associated with that night - she finds herself deliberately trying to go somewhere else inside her mind, to blank out, to leave her body entirely. This deliberate dissociation brings momentary relief, but it keeps the memory from being processed or contextualised, so that it remains raw and fragmentary, ready to be triggered again at the next encounter with water or with anything that rhymes with that night.

The maintaining cycle has tightened over months. Because the memory remains unintegrated, ordinary sensory input continues to carry disproportionate threat. Marisol is on high alert for unexpected sounds at work - a dropped tray, a door slamming - and her nervous system reads each one as potential warning. Poor sleep compounds this: she lies awake most nights, startling at the sound of rain on the window, and arrives at the clinic already depleted. In this hypervigilant state, even mild triggers feel dangerous, which means she encounters the nausea and the emotional flooding more frequently, which in turn drives her back toward deliberate dissociation and past-dwelling - hours spent mourning the woman she was before the storm, competent and unafraid. She has begun avoiding going out beyond what work strictly requires. Grocery trips, social invitations, a standing dinner with her adult daughter - all quietly cancelled. Her daughter has noticed. A colleague asked last month whether she was all right. Marisol said yes.

What finally brought her to seek help was a session with a patient - a young man recovering from a knee replacement - who mentioned offhandedly that he had grown up near the Withlacoochee River. The name alone was enough. She excused herself, went to the staff bathroom, and sat on the floor for fifteen minutes. She is most afraid, she says, that she will never feel safe anywhere again. What she is hoping for, more than anything, is to be able to walk past water without her body remembering.
